note: Six stories. The paper skipped 14 to 22 November and does not try to catch up. Search returned little dependable UK or world reporting dated 21 to 23 November, and BBC, Reuters and Guardian pages could not be opened, so this is a shorter edition with no UK or world stories rather than a padded one. Some AI and security items rest on a single secondary outlet and say so.

stories.headline: Verstappen wins Las Vegas Grand Prix from pole as Norris and Piastri complete a McLaren double podium
stories.standfirst: Russell and Verstappen traded the lead before Russell hit the wall and finished ninth; Hamilton and Leclerc each took 10-second penalties.
body: Read Motorsport and PlanetF1 agree on the order: Max Verstappen won from pole, then Lando Norris (+0.639s), Oscar Piastri (+1.529s), Kimi Antonelli (+2.574s), Pierre Gasly (+2.927s), Franco Colapinto (+7.955s), Lewis Hamilton (+12.795s), Carlos Sainz (+12.938s), George Russell (+13.192s) and Charles Leclerc (+17.554s). Read Motorsport reports that Piastri started 17th after a 10-place grid penalty, Antonelli sixth and Sainz 20th. Neither page gives tyre compounds or stint lengths. PlanetF1 says Red Bull double-stacked Verstappen and Isack Hadjar at their stops.

PlanetF1 describes a race in which Russell and Verstappen repeatedly swapped the lead. Russell then hit the barrier, at Turn 5 according to PlanetF1 and three laps from the end according to Read Motorsport, and dropped to ninth. PlanetF1 reports a Safety Car on lap 19 after Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara collided; Read Motorsport does not mention one. Perez and Arvid Lindblad retired on both accounts, and PlanetF1 says Lindblad spun behind the Safety Car.

Hamilton and Leclerc each received a 10-second penalty. Neither page cites a regulation, and the reasons differ: PlanetF1 says Hamilton's was for his pass on Norris and Leclerc's for colliding with Hamilton, while Read Motorsport says both were for contact. PlanetF1 also says Piastri passed Norris for fifth before the finish, which does not fit the classification above and is not reconciled in either piece.

The pages disagree on the back of the field. PlanetF1 says Liam Lawson (fuel leak) and Alex Albon did not make the start and that Lawson finished a lap down; Read Motorsport lists Lawson 15th and only Albon as a non-starter. They also differ on where Hadjar rejoined, 19th or 14th. Neither page gives the fastest lap.

sources.name: PlanetF1, Las Vegas Grand Prix race report
Read Motorsport, Las Vegas GP race results

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis in Lean; the formal artifact is certified, the mathematics is not yet explained
stories.standfirst: The proof is about 17 million lines of Lean with no conventional paper, and sources differ on its scope and on Claude's role.
body: The Next Web, citing Bloomberg, reports that Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, wrote on his website that working with Claude he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. Unite.AI dates his announcement to 20 November. Both say the result exists only as a Lean formalisation of roughly 17 million lines, with no conventional paper. Neither names the Claude model used, and The Next Web says Anthropic declined to comment to Bloomberg.

Unite.AI reports that the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative endorsed a community certification on 21 November. It covers the formal artifact: a check that the stated theorem matches Mathlib's definition of the Riemann hypothesis, kernel checks and an axiom audit showing only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. MIT's Andrew Sutherland reports that all 175,187 modules compiled on Lean and Mathlib 4.33.1, and The Next Web quotes him putting the chance of error at roughly zero. Unite.AI lists checks still outstanding at the time: default and paranoid kernel runs, the full lake comparator run, runs on unsandboxed machines and a comparison of the export hash with a sandboxed build.

The pages differ on scope. The Next Web says the work also covers the generalised hypothesis, while Unite.AI limits it to Dirichlet L-functions and excludes Dedekind, Hecke and general automorphic L-functions. They also differ on Claude's contribution: The Next Web says Claude did much of the work and quotes Alpoge saying it far outpaced him near the end, while Unite.AI stresses that he guided the work from a toy setting and says it does not show an autonomous solution.

The Next Web says the proof is not yet accepted, and Imperial's Kevin Buzzard is reported as saying nobody yet understands what it shows. Alpoge plans to understand, simplify and explain the argument, and that write-up is pending. Unite.AI's byline says its articles are AI-generated and editorially reviewed, and neither page links a primary Lean repository that was opened for this edition.

stories.headline: OpenRouter drops three inference providers and 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention after Dragos canary research; Together AI discloses a separate credential leak
stories.standfirst: Dragos seeded about two million canary prompts and found data leaking from at least three AI providers; the account here rests on Unite.AI summaries.
body: Unite.AI, summarising research Dragos published on 19 November, says Dragos sent about two million prompts carrying unique URLs and canary credentials to AI services between July and November 2026, then monitored for use. It traced about 2,000 inference routes, several hundred of which included an unidentified system. The largest compromise was a couple of hundred seeded AWS keys sent in late October, which were then used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls. At least three providers leaked data; the article does not name them beyond linking notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI.

OpenRouter said it had off-boarded three inference providers, which it does not name, and removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, restoring it only after assurances and validation. It notified potentially affected customers and says OpenRouter itself was not breached. The article is dated 21 November but says OpenRouter announced on 22 November, which is not reconciled. Its linked provider notices describe separate incidents: Phala had an exposure window from 21 October to 8 November in which an attacker chained a legacy service with loopback trust, and Novita had a routing misconfiguration from 28 May to 11 November that sent some MiniMax requests to MiniMax's own API.

Together AI's disclosure is a different mechanism. A coding agent committed a credential for a private Hugging Face repository to the public xorl GitHub repo. That repository held stored prompt samples for a subset of serverless requests. Automated scanning found the commit and it was reverted, but the credential was used during the exposure window, mainly 24 June and 4, 8 and 14 July. Together says five Dragos canary credentials were involved, review of sensitive personal data continues, and it is moving to scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on every pull request, rules for AI coding agents and Zero Data Retention by default for new accounts. A forensic firm and law enforcement are involved. No CVEs are given in either article, and the Dragos report itself was not opened.

stories.headline: Architect Labs says AI agents designed Frostbite, an interaction-net CPU, claiming 4.59 times the performance per watt of an in-order core in pre-silicon tests
stories.standfirst: The results come from a simulated 7nm design with a 16-tile layout; nothing has been fabricated and the baseline core is unnamed.
body: Tom's Hardware reports that Palo Alto startup Architect Labs designed and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set, using AI agents. Programs compile to interaction nets, which the company describes as multithreading for free, with no threads, locks or out-of-order hardware. The design is a 4 by 4 grid of 16 identical tiles on an on-chip network, each with local memory, and idle tiles can steal work. The benchmarked configuration is a cluster of 4 tiles plus 4 L3 nodes.

All figures are pre-silicon. The 7nm design reached 800 MHz in early synthesis and 500 MHz after final layout. Architect Labs claims 4.59 times the performance per watt of a silicon-proven dual-issue in-order core as the geometric mean over 25 workloads: 6.02 times on the 10 workloads used for tuning and 3.83 times on 15 held-out ones, from 23.12 times on conv2d down to 1.15 times on recursive Fibonacci. Performance per area averages 8.77 times. The baseline is unnamed for legal reasons; commenters guess an Arm Cortex-A55, which the article does not confirm.

On the process, the agents started with no architectural priors and a 141-page specification was deleted once the first RTL existed. The spec language, ASL, translates to the Lean proof checker. A software model called Arcmodel, about 200 times faster than RTL simulation, initially mis-estimated power by up to about 250 per cent, and the agent swarms tried 58 changes and kept 37. Comparisons with out-of-order CPUs and on SPEC and PARSEC are planned, along with an FPGA playground and a preliminary operating system; no OS is described as running. The Tom's Hardware text was only partly readable for this edition, and the process and benchmark details come from a summary of its latter part.

stories.headline: Sarvam-105B-1711: 105B-parameter mixture-of-experts checkpoint with 10.3B active parameters and a 4-bit build that fits one 96 GB GPU
stories.standfirst: The vendor-run benchmarks show large gains over the February checkpoint on instruction following and tool use.
body: Unite.AI reports that Sarvam has released Sarvam-105B-1711, a post-training update of its 105B mixture-of-experts model with 10.3B active parameters. Context is 160K tokens, extended by continued pretraining on 330B tokens over a little more than seven days on 512 B200 GPUs. The licence is Apache-2.0 according to the repository tag the article cites, which was not independently checked. The article says the model targets Indian languages without listing them.

Two formats are offered: BF16 weights for fine-tuning and post-training, and a 65 GB NVFP4 4-bit build; MXFP8 was used for training only. The NVFP4 checkpoint fits a single 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and decodes at 99 tokens per second for one user with a 10K-token prompt. Sarvam's own figure is 6,067 decode tokens per second per B200 at 64 concurrent requests. The model card, per the article, specifies vLLM 0.33.0, thinking on by default, and temperature 1.0 with thinking or 0.6 without. Sarvam quotes a blended price of $0.15 per million tokens.

All benchmarks are Sarvam's own runs. IFBench rises from 32.5 for the February checkpoint to 82.5, and Tau2 customer-service tool use from 46.2 to 85.5, with pass^4 at 69.5 per cent against 63.9 for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 62.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On an internal Indic suite judged by Gemini 3.1 Pro the score goes from 30.1 to 79.1. Across eight conversational-agent benchmarks the NVFP4 build averages 73.9, up from 42.6, against 74.0 for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 73.0 for Gemma 4 31B.

stories.headline: Signal blocks in-app screenshots on Android and iOS by default, calling the fix incomplete
stories.standfirst: President Meredith Whittaker describes operating-system AI agents as an existential threat to Signal's privacy guarantees.
body: TechCrunch reports that Signal now restricts screenshots inside its mobile apps on Android and iOS, having already blocked them by default in its Windows app. Users can switch the restriction off, though Whittaker says doing so would break Signal's privacy guarantees. The article gives no version numbers and does not describe the mechanism, such as which OS interface is used, and Signal's own blog post was not opened.

Whittaker calls operating-system-level agentic AI an existential threat and says such features undermine Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy on Windows, Android, macOS and iOS. She also calls the screenshot block incomplete because it does not address other, less visible ways AI agents could reach application data. TechCrunch's page is stamped 21 November while saying Signal announced the change on Friday, so the announcement date is unclear.

briefs.text: Hackers breached the FBI's NCIC law enforcement database, the third FBI hack this year, with the extent of data taken unknown; separately the US Department of Agriculture's farmer payment system was breached and taken offline, according to this week's security newsletter.
An extortion group stole names, emails and some phone numbers of about 16,000 high-net-worth Chase customers from a third-party marketing vendor, per the same newsletter.
A breach at French postal subsidiary Maileva exposed names and addresses of 22 million people, according to the same newsletter.
